III Models


System Model.
 In our system, there are three types of participants:
(i) The data owner 𝒪\mathcal{O} who owns some data;
(ii) The data user 𝒰\mathcal{U} who would like to access 𝒪\mathcal{O}’s data;
(iii) The storage provider 𝒮\mathcal{S} that provides storage facilities to store 𝒪\mathcal{O}’s data remotely.
Our system permits data storage, sharing, and access between these participants while, at the same time, recording all the data operations in a distributed audit log for auditability.
A Privacy-preserving and Immutable Audit Log (PIAL) scheme consists of the following PPT algorithms –



• 

(ℒ,𝗉𝗉)←𝖨𝗇𝗂𝗍⁡(1λ,N)(\mathcal{L},\mathsf{pp})\leftarrow\mathsf{Init}(1^{\lambda},N): Given a security parameter λ\lambda, and the maximum number of supported operations NN, it outputs an initial distributed audit log ℒ\mathcal{L} and public parameters 𝗉𝗉\mathsf{pp}.

• 

(𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋)←𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗋⁡(1λ)(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}})\leftarrow\mathsf{Register}(1^{\lambda}): Given a security parameter λ\lambda, it outputs an address-key pair (𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋)(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}) as an identifier for the participant.

• 

(𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋,𝗍𝗑𝗌𝗍𝗋)←𝖲𝗍𝗈𝗋𝖾⁡(D,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,𝗉𝗉CLOSE(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}},\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{str}})\leftarrow\mathsf{Store}(D,\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}},\mathsf{pp}): Given data DD, 𝒪\mathcal{O}’s private identity 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}}, 𝒮\mathcal{S}’s public identity 𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}}, it outputs a store token 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}} and a store record 𝗍𝗑𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{str}}.

• 

(𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇,𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇)←𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋⁡(𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,𝗉𝗉)(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}},\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}})\leftarrow\mathsf{AssignOwner}(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}},\mathsf{pp}):
Given 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}}, 𝒮\mathcal{S}’s private identity 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}}, and 𝒪\mathcal{O}’s public identity 𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}}, it outputs an ownership token 𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}}, which permits 𝒪\mathcal{O} to share her data stored on 𝒮\mathcal{S} later, and create a record of ownership 𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}.

• 

(𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋,𝗍𝗑𝗌𝗁𝗋)←𝖲𝗁𝖺𝗋𝖾⁡(𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒰,𝗍𝗌,𝗉𝗉)(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}},\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{shr}})\leftarrow\mathsf{Share}(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{U}},\mathsf{ts},\mathsf{pp}): Given 𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}}, 𝒪\mathcal{O}’s private identity 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O}}, 𝒰\mathcal{U}’s public identity 𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒰\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{U}}, a share expiry timestamp 𝗍𝗌>0\mathsf{ts}>0, it outputs a data share token 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}} that is only valid up to 𝗍𝗌\mathsf{ts}, and a record of share 𝗍𝗑𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{shr}}.

• 

(𝗍𝗄𝖺𝖼𝖼,𝗍𝗑𝖺𝖼𝖼)←𝖠𝖼𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌(𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒰,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮.𝗉𝗉)(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{acc}},\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{acc}})\leftarrow\mathsf{Access}(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{U}},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}}.\mathsf{pp}): Given 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}}, 𝒰\mathcal{U}’s private identity 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒰\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{U}}, 𝒮\mathcal{S}’s public identity 𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}}, it outputs a data access token 𝗍𝗄𝖺𝖼𝖼\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{acc}} (if 𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗁𝗋\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{shr}} is not expired) and a record of access 𝗍𝗑𝖺𝖼𝖼\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{acc}}.

• 

{0,1}←𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒𝖫𝗈𝗀⁡(𝗍𝗑,ℒ,𝗉𝗉)\{0,1\}\leftarrow\mathsf{VerifyLog}(\mathsf{tx},\mathcal{L},\mathsf{pp}): Given a record 𝗍𝗑\mathsf{tx} and audit log ℒ\mathcal{L}, it outputs 11 if the record is valid else 00.




Threat and Security Models.

We assume participants do not trust each other, i.e., they can behave maliciously toward the records created by other participants.
The adversary is curious about the record content, e.g., who is the owner of a particular data, whom the data is shared with or accessed by, and what data is being shared or accessed.
The adversary may also attempt to modify the record to compromise validity or to gain unauthorized access.
We aim to achieve integrity and confidentiality properties for the audit log via record non-malleability and audit log indistinguishability as follows.


Definition 1 (Record Non-Malleability).

Let Π\Pi be a candidate PIAL scheme. Consider experiment NMGameΠ,𝒜​(λ)\texttt{NMGame}_{\Pi,\mathcal{A}}(\lambda) between the adversary 𝒜\mathcal{A} and the challenger 𝒞\mathcal{C}. 𝒞\mathcal{C} samples 𝗉𝗉←𝖨𝗇𝗂𝗍⁡(1λ)\mathsf{pp}\leftarrow\mathsf{Init}(1^{\lambda}) and sends 𝗉𝗉\mathsf{pp} to 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Then, 𝒞\mathcal{C} initializes a PIAL oracle 𝒪𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}} using 𝗉𝗉\mathsf{pp} with audit log ℒ\mathcal{L}. At each time step, 𝒜\mathcal{A} adaptively specifies a query q∈{𝖢𝗋𝖾𝖺𝗍𝖾𝖠𝖽𝖽𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗌q\in\{\mathsf{CreateAddress}, 𝖲𝗍𝗈𝗋𝖾\mathsf{Store}, 𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋\mathsf{AssignOwner}, 𝖲𝗁𝖺𝗋𝖾\mathsf{Share}, 𝖠𝖼𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌}\mathsf{Access}\} to 𝒞\mathcal{C}. 𝒞\mathcal{C} forwards qq to 𝒪𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}}, receives a response and forwards it to 𝒜\mathcal{A}. 𝒞\mathcal{C} also provides the view of ℒ\mathcal{L} to 𝒜\mathcal{A}. 𝒜\mathcal{A} outputs a record 𝗍𝗑∗\mathsf{tx}^{*} and let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be the set of records with the same type of 𝗍𝗑∗\mathsf{tx}^{*} that 𝒪𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}} generates during the query phase.


If there exists a record 𝗍𝗑∈𝒯\mathsf{tx}\in\mathcal{T} created in response to a query, 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins and outputs 1 iff the following conditions hold – (i) m∗≠mm^{*}\neq m; (ii) 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒𝖫𝗈𝗀⁡(𝗍𝗑∗,𝗉𝗉,ℒ′)=1\mathsf{VerifyLog}(\mathsf{tx}^{*},\mathsf{pp},\mathcal{L}^{\prime})=1, where ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} is the state of the audit log preceding 𝗍𝗑\mathsf{tx}; iii) if 𝗍𝗑∗\mathsf{tx}^{*} is a record of ownership, 𝗌𝗇∗=𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn}^{*}=\mathsf{sn}. Otherwise, it outputs 0.


Π\Pi is said to achieve record non-malleability if 𝖯𝗋[NMGameΠ,𝒜(λ)=1]≤𝗇𝖾𝗀𝗅(λ)\mathsf{Pr}[{\texttt{NMGame}}_{\Pi,\mathcal{A}}(\lambda)=1]\leq\mathsf{negl}(\lambda).



Definition 2 (Audit Log Indistinguishability).

Let Π\Pi be a candidate PIAL scheme. Consider experiment IndGameΠ,𝒜​(λ)\texttt{IndGame}_{\Pi,\mathcal{A}}(\lambda) between 𝒜\mathcal{A} and 𝒞\mathcal{C}. 𝒞\mathcal{C} first samples a random bit b←${0,1}b\xleftarrow{\$}\{0,1\}, 𝗉𝗉←𝖢𝗈𝗆.𝒢⁡(1λ)\mathsf{pp}\leftarrow\mathsf{Com}.\mathcal{G}(1^{\lambda}) and initializes two PIAL oracles 𝒪0𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}}_{0} and 𝒪1𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}}_{1}, where each oracle 𝒪i𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}}_{i} has a separate audit log ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i} as well as internal variables. At each time step, 𝒜\mathcal{A} adaptively specifies two queries Q,Q′Q,Q^{\prime} of the same type (one of 𝖲𝗍𝗈𝗋𝖾,𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋,𝖲𝗁𝖺𝗋𝖾,𝖠𝖼𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌\mathsf{Store},\mathsf{AssignOwner},\mathsf{Share},\mathsf{Access}).
𝒞\mathcal{C} forwards QQ to 𝒪0𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}}_{0}, Q′Q^{\prime} to 𝒪1𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}}_{1} and receives the corresponding answers R0,R1R_{0},R_{1}. 𝒞\mathcal{C} forwards (Rb,R1−b)(R_{b},R_{1-b}) to 𝒜\mathcal{A}. 𝒞\mathcal{C} also provides to 𝒜\mathcal{A} two ledgers ℒ𝗅𝖾𝖿𝗍=ℒb\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{left}}=\mathcal{L}_{b}, ℒ𝗋𝗂𝗀𝗁𝗍=ℒ1−b\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{right}}=\mathcal{L}_{1-b}, where ℒb\mathcal{L}_{b} is the current audit log in 𝒪b𝖯𝖨𝖠𝖫\mathcal{O}^{\mathsf{PIAL}}_{b}. 𝒜\mathcal{A} outputs a bit b′∈{0,1}b^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}. 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins if b′=bb^{\prime}=b and outputs 11 else 0.


Π\Pi is said to achieve audit log indistinguishability if
𝖯𝗋[IndGameΠ,𝒜(λ)=1]≤12+𝗇𝖾𝗀𝗅(λ)\mathsf{Pr}[{\texttt{IndGame}}_{\Pi,\mathcal{A}}(\lambda)=1]\leq\frac{1}{2}+\mathsf{negl}(\lambda).

V Security Analysis


Theorem 1.

𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} satisfies record non-malleability by Definition 1.



Proof (sketch).

Let Q𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗋={1λ,1λ,…}Q_{\mathsf{Register}}=\{1^{\lambda},1^{\lambda},\dotsc\} be the queries by 𝒜\mathcal{A} to 𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗋\mathsf{Register} and R𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗋={(𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,1,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,1),(𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,2,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,2),…}R_{\mathsf{Register}}=\{(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S},1},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S},1}),(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S},2},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S},2}),\dotsc\} be 𝒞\mathcal{C}’s response.


Without loss of generality, let
Q𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋={(𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋1,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,1,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,1,𝗉𝗉),(𝗍𝗄𝗌𝗍𝗋2,𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮,2,𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒪,2,𝗉𝗉),,…}Q_{\mathsf{AssignOwner}}=\{(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}}^{1},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S},1},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O},1},\mathsf{pp}),(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{str}}^{2},\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S},2},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{O},2},\mathsf{pp}),,\dotsc\} be the queries created by 𝒜\mathcal{A} and R𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋={(𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇1,𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇1),(𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇2,𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇2),…}R_{\mathsf{AssignOwner}}=\{(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}}^{1},\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}^{1}),(\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}}^{2},\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}^{2}),\dotsc\} be the response by 𝒞\mathcal{C}. 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins the experiment NMGame when it outputs a record 𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇∗\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*} such that (i) m∗≠mm^{*}\neq m, where mm is the message in some 𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇∈R𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}\in R_{\mathsf{AssignOwner}}; (ii) 𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒𝖫𝗈𝗀⁡(𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇∗,ℒ′,𝗉𝗉)=1\mathsf{VerifyLog}(\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*},\mathcal{L}^{\prime},\mathsf{pp})=1, where ℒ′\mathcal{L}^{\prime} is the state of the audit log preceding 𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}; (iii) 𝗌𝗇∗=𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn}^{*}=\mathsf{sn} iff 𝗍𝗑∗\mathsf{tx}^{*} is an ownership record.


Assume that 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins by creating a record 𝗍𝗑𝗈𝗐𝗇∗=(𝗋𝗍𝗌𝗍𝗋∗,𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀∗,σ∗,𝗌𝗇∗,𝖼𝗆𝗈𝗐𝗇∗,h∗,π𝗈𝗐𝗇∗,𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇∗)\mathsf{tx}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*}=(\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{str}}^{*},\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}^{*},\sigma^{*},\mathsf{sn}^{*},\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*},h^{*},\pi_{\mathsf{own}}^{*},\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*}) with proof instance x∗=(𝗋𝗍𝗌𝗍𝗋∗,𝗌𝗇∗,𝖼𝗆𝗈𝗐𝗇∗,h∗)x^{*}=(\mathsf{rt}_{\mathsf{str}}^{*},\mathsf{sn}^{*},\mathsf{cm}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*},h^{*}) and m∗=x∗||h𝗌𝗂𝗀∗|​|π𝗈𝗐𝗇∗||𝗍𝗄𝗈𝗐𝗇∗m^{*}=x^{*}||h_{\mathsf{sig}}^{*}||\pi_{\mathsf{own}}^{*}||\mathsf{tk}_{\mathsf{own}}^{*}. We consider the following events.


E1:E_{1}: 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins, and there exists 𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀∈R𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}\in R_{\mathsf{AssignOwner}} such that 𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀∗=𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}^{*}=\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}. To win, 𝒜\mathcal{A} produces σ∗\sigma^{*} such that Σ.𝖵𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒⁡(𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀∗,m∗,σ∗)=1\Sigma.\mathsf{Verify}(\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}^{*},m^{*},\sigma^{*})=1, m∗≠mm^{*}\neq m and 𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀∗=𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}^{*}=\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}. However, due to the SUF-CMA property of the signature scheme [22], this happens with negligible probability.


E2:E_{2}: 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins, E1E_{1} does not occur, and there exists 𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀∈R𝖠𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗇𝖮𝗐𝗇𝖾𝗋\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}\in R_{\mathsf{AssignOwner}} such that h𝗌𝗂𝗀∗=h𝗌𝗂𝗀h^{*}_{\mathsf{sig}}=h_{\mathsf{sig}}. When 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins, it crafts a h𝗌𝗂𝗀∗=h𝗌𝗂𝗀h^{*}_{\mathsf{sig}}=h_{\mathsf{sig}} when 𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀∗≠𝗉𝗄𝗌𝗂𝗀\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}^{*}\neq\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{sig}}. However, the hash function [23] is collision-resistant, a contradiction.


E3:E_{3}: 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins, (E1,E2)(E_{1},E_{2}) do not occur and h∗=𝖯𝖱𝖥(𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮∗||h𝗌𝗂𝗀∗)h^{*}=\mathsf{PRF}(\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}^{*}}||h^{*}_{\mathsf{sig}}) for some 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮∗∈R𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗋\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}^{*}}\in R_{\mathsf{Register}}. Due to the one-wayness property of 𝖯𝖱𝖥\mathsf{PRF} (used to generate 𝗉𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮∗\mathsf{pk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}^{*}}), 𝒜\mathcal{A} will not be able to deduce 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮∗\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}^{*}} and generates h∗h^{*} with a random key. However, due to indistinguishability property of 𝖯𝖱𝖥\mathsf{PRF} (used to generate h∗h^{*}), 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins negligbly.


E4:E_{4}: 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins, (E1,E2,E3)(E_{1},E_{2},E_{3}) do not occur, 𝗍𝗑∗\mathsf{tx}^{*} is an ownership record and h∗≠𝖯𝖱𝖥(𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮∗||h𝗌𝗂𝗀∗)h^{*}\neq\mathsf{PRF}(\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}^{*}}||h^{*}_{\mathsf{sig}}) for all 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮∗∈R𝖱𝖾𝗀𝗂𝗌𝗍𝖾𝗋\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}^{*}}\in R_{\mathsf{Register}}. If 𝒜\mathcal{A} wins, it outputs a modified record such that 𝗌𝗇∗=𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn}^{*}=\mathsf{sn}. However, since in E4E_{4} 𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮∗≠𝗌𝗄𝖺𝖽𝗋𝒮\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}^{*}}\neq\mathsf{sk}_{\mathsf{adr}}^{\mathcal{S}}, it means that to generate 𝗌𝗇∗\mathsf{sn}^{*}, 𝒜\mathcal{A} found a collision in the 𝖯𝖱𝖥\mathsf{PRF} needed to generate 𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn} which occurs with negligible probability due to the collision-resistant property of the 𝖯𝖱𝖥\mathsf{PRF} function used to generate 𝗌𝗇\mathsf{sn}. ∎



Theorem 2.

𝖧𝖺𝗋𝗉𝗈𝖼𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾𝗌\mathsf{Harpocrates} satisfies audit log indistinguishability by Definition 2



Proof (sketch).

4.3 Publishing Mechanism


The publishing mechanism is the main influence on choosing CRSet capacity nm​a​xn_{max}.
To maintain perfect deniability, an issuer must update, i.e., recreate and publish, the filter cascade in regular intervals, regardless of whether there are new revocations (e.g., every 24 hours).
The cascade should be published on a decentralized storage system, for which we use the Ethereum blockchain’s blob-carrying transactions [15] due to their comparatively low cost for writing data to a public, distributed system.
To optimize space usage on blobs, the padded size nm​a​xn_{max} should be chosen such that the total bit size of the cascade is a multiple of the blob size.
Building on cascade size calculations from [16], for one blob, CRSet can support nm​a​x≈128​K​B/6​b≈170.666n_{max}\approx 128KB/6b\approx 170.666 VCs.
Blobs are officially kept for a limited time [15], which works well with regular updates where only the latest one is relevant for revocation checks.

keytrans_architecture11.section-7.1:
7.1. Transparency Log Misbehavior
        
If the transparency log does not execute an operation correctly, then one of the
following occurs:¶


            The user detects the error immediately and rejects the proof.¶

          
            The user permanently enters an invalid state. That is, the user accepts a
result that is inconsistent with what the transparency log has shown other
users, such as a forked view of the log or a version of a label that the
transparency log later attempts to remove. Since users require all
subsequent queries to prove consistency with previous ones, the transparency
log is unable to reconcile the user's view with that of other users. This is
intentional, as it ensures the misbehavior is eventually detected, either by
background monitoring or by the mechanisms described in Section 3.3.
Importantly, this means that users must stay online for a bounded amount of
time after entering an invalid state for it to be successfully detected.¶

          
            Instead of executing a query incorrectly, the transparency log can attempt to
prevent the user from learning about more recent states of the log. This
would allow the log to continue executing queries correctly, but on stale
versions of data. To prevent this, applications configure an upper bound on
how stale a query response can be without being rejected.¶

        
The security of a transparency log depends naturally on the security of the
cryptographic primitives that it's configured to use, as well as the deployment
mode that the transparency log relies on:¶


            Third-Party Management and Third-Party Auditing require an assumption that the
service operator and the third-party manager or auditor do not collude to
trick users into accepting malicious results.¶

          
            Contact Monitoring requires an assumption that all users that look up a label
complete any necessary monitoring afterwards.¶

        
In short, assuming that the underlying cryptographic primitives used are secure,
any deployment-specific assumptions hold (such as non-collusion), and that a
label owner's devices don't go offline for longer than the maximum lifetime of
log entries, then any attempt by the transparency log to present inconsistent
views of a label to different users is always detected within a bounded amount
of time. The parameters that determine the maximum amount of time before such
misbehavior is detected are as follows:¶


            The configured maximum amount of time by which a query response can be stale.¶

          
            The configured Reasonable Monitoring Window (see Section 4),
weighed against how frequently users execute background monitoring in
practice.¶

          
            For logs that use the Contact Monitoring deployment mode: how frequently users
engage in out-of-band communication.¶

          
            For logs that use the Third-Party Auditing deployment mode: the configured
maximum acceptable lag for an auditor.¶

          
            For logs that use the Third-Party Management deployment mode: the amount of
lag, or potential inefficacy, of the service operator's approach to detecting
forks.¶

        
Ultimately, a transparency log can always refuse to answer requests that would
reveal its own misbehavior. This includes refusing direct requests, requests
made over an anonymous channel, and requests for the specific tree heads users
need to efficiently gossip peer-to-peer. Similarly, a transparency log can
refuse to apply updates to a user's own label, such as replacing a compromised
public key. A user's persistent inability to perform monitoring, engage in out-of-band
communication, or update their own label is indistinguishable from transparency
log misbehavior and should be reported to the user as such.¶
keytrans_architecture11.section-7.2:
7.2. State Loss
        
The security of KT often depends on the ability of users to maintain robust
local state. Users that lose their state in a Contact Monitoring or Third-Party
Auditing deployment will have a correspondingly reduced ability to detect if
they were shown a fork, or if the transparency log later obscured data that they
consumed. State loss can occur, for example, when a user's device is lost,
replaced, or reset, when the application is reinstalled or its data is cleared,
or when the user begins using a new device without transferring state from an
old one.¶
In a Contact Monitoring deployment mode, state loss reduces a user's ability to
detect misbehavior if it occurs after the user consumes a version of a label
that was created either within the Reasonable Monitoring Window, or within a
portion of the log that was insufficiently gossiped. In a Third-Party Auditing
deployment mode, the same is true for a version of a label that was created
within the auditor's maximum acceptable lag.¶
Applications should consider the nature of possible state loss in their clients
when configuring a transparency log and ensure that the relevant
protocol parameters are set in a way that appropriately mitigates this risk.
For example, in a Contact Monitoring deployment, the Reasonable Monitoring
Window and the duration between out-of-band communication attempts should be
much less than the typical time between state loss events. Similarly, in a
Third-Party Auditing deployment, the maximum acceptable lag for an auditor
should be much less than the typical time between state loss events. This
minimizes the likelihood that a state loss event could be useful to a
misbehaving transparency log.¶
In applications where client state is typically ephemeral (like a web page), or
where state loss could possibly be triggered adversarially (for example, by the
service operator forcing a user to log out and re-register), a Third-Party
Management deployment mode is recommended. Alternatively, applications could
also consider implementing a policy of not consuming label-version pairs that
were inserted too recently. Once a label-version pair is outside of the
Reasonable Monitoring Window in a Contact Monitoring deployment, or beyond the
maximum acceptable auditor lag in a Third-Party Auditing deployment, the risks
associated with state loss are often already sufficiently mitigated.¶
keytrans_architecture11.section-8.2:
8.2. Population-Level Metrics
        
Service operators also expect to be able to control sensitive population-level
metrics about their users. These metrics include the size of their user base, the
frequency with which new users join, and the frequency with which existing users
update their labels.¶
KT allows a service operator to obscure the size of its user base by batch
inserting a large number of fake label-version pairs when a transparency log is
first initialized. Similarly, KT also allows a service operator to obscure the
rate at which "real" changes are made to the transparency log by padding "real"
changes with the insertion of other fake label-version pairs, such that it
creates the outside appearance of a constant baseline rate of insertions.¶
